### The last practical wall, named

The daily is https and the daemons are http on a tailnet. An https page asking
for `http://127.0.0.1` is a mixed-content request and a browser may block it -
which looks exactly like a provider that never answered. The tool prints that
warning with the way out: serve the built page over http from the same machine
(`BLWP_PAGE=http://host:8000`), or put the daemons behind https. Nothing in the
protocol changes either way; it is where the page is served from.

### And the page is served from the same machine, so nothing is mixed content

The wall named at the end of the last slice is closed. The daily is https and
these daemons are http, and an https page fetching `http://127.0.0.1` is a
mixed-content request a browser may refuse - a refusal that looks exactly like
a chain provider which never answered, which is the worst kind of wall: it
fails where the evidence points somewhere else.

## Item 29, slice 1: the dealer is checked at handout, not at settlement

23.1 asks for verifiable secret sharing and says what verifiable means: "each
node can confirm its share is consistent WITHOUT reconstructing P". What was
there was a hash commitment per share - it catches a share corrupted or swapped
in transit, and it says nothing at all about the DEALER, because the dealer
wrote both sides of it. `shares.js` said so in its own header and named the
price. This is that price paid.

### The figure

The two-polynomial dealer the suite already builds: three of the seven seats
are handed a share from a second polynomial.

    with the hash commitments alone   0 of 7 refused at handout
    with the polynomial published     3 of 7 refused at handout, seats 5, 6, 7
    honest dealer                     0 of 7 refused, 21 of 21 subsets open P

Measured twice: in `protocol/test/shares.test.js` over Z_n, and in
`blwp-node/test/shares-feldman.test.js` over real secp256k1. Before this, that
handout reached settlement and 0 of the 21 five-subsets could open the
committed preimage - a stake nobody could ever settle, dealt by the player who
staked it. Now the entry never becomes an entry.

### The group, and the constant that had to move with it

Daniel's pick: injected secp256k1, the curve this system already trusts for
bonds and BIP-340. No second group. Commitments are 33-byte compressed points -
compressed and not x-only, because g^s = product only holds up to the sign and
the sign is part of what is being checked. `packages/protocol` still carries no
curve: `pointFromScalar` and `combinePoints` are injected the way `deriveCensus`
already takes `tweakPoint` and `combine`, and the daemon's copies live beside
them in `blwp-node/src/curve.js`.

THE SHARING FIELD IS NOW n, secp256k1's order, and it could not stay 2^521 - 1:
Feldman's exponents have to be scalars of the group its commitments live in.
The order is below 2^256, so the room a 32-byte preimage used to have is gone.
A preimage at or above n is REFUSED AT GENERATION by name - reducing it would
change the number whose hash the player already put in the Entry Contract, so
the shares would open a preimage the payment hash does not name.

A SIDE EFFECT WORTH RECORDING, measured rather than guessed. In the old
521-bit field a mixed interpolation almost never landed inside 32 bytes, so
most bad subsets were refused for their SIZE and only two came back as
plausible wrong preimages. In a 256-bit field every element fits:

    mixed subsets: 21 well-formed and wrong, 0 too big, 21 caught by the commitment

The size accident is gone, and the reconstruction-side commitment check - the
"quieter half" closed earlier - is now the only thing standing between a
settlement committee and a wrong preimage that looks exactly like a right one.
It catches all 21.

actually asks, and today no seat asks anywhere but in a test.

So 29 is NOT closed here, and the missing piece is named rather than parked:
the commitments have to reach a seat. That means the published shares get a
place - 23.1's `vss_shares_ref` - and something on the daemon or the client
runs `checkHandout` before an entry is accepted. It is contract surface, which
is letter 16's family: adding a field to the Entry Contract moves every entry
id and every fixture that carries one, so it is Daniel's call whether that is
slice 2 of 29 or its own letter.

### Encrypting one share to each member: M3, and why that is not parking it

23.1 step 2 also says the player "encrypts one share to each settlement-
committee member". That is confidentiality, and what it protects is the stake:
five shares in the clear are a preimage anybody can rebuild. M2 asks for no
money and distributes none (Daniel 2026-09-08 12:09), so in M2 there is no
stake behind P and nothing to take by reading a share. It becomes REQUIRED at
the same moment the hold invoice does - the first letter where P is worth sats
- and it needs a key agreement nobody has chosen, which is a decision and not a
task. Feldman does not make it more urgent: C_0 = g^P is published by design
and telling P from it is the discrete log of the curve.

The property 29 buys - a dealer cannot hand out shares that no five seats can
open - holds whether or not the shares are encrypted.

## Item 29, slice 2: the check is in force, and a seat is the one asking

### What is on the wire now

    Entry Contract   + vssSharesRef, 32 bytes, IN THE SIGNED BYTES
    TYPE_VSS_HANDOUT 0x12, authority: true - it gates play, so it decides
                     something, and the frames guard made me say so (17 -> 18)
    handout.js       encode / decode / handoutId / acceptHandout
    daemon           POST /handout  checks and keeps, GET /handout serves back
                     POST /entry    refuses a ref it never accepted

The reference is the tagged hash of the WHOLE handout, so it binds the shares
and the polynomial together: a dealer cannot swap the polynomial under a
reference that was already signed.

32 zero bytes is a real value meaning "this entry publishes no shares", which
is every entry in M2 - there is no stake behind the preimage yet. It is not a
default the encoder supplies: a caller says which it means, so an entry that
forgot the field and an entry that has none are never the same bytes.

## Item 32, slice 1: which block seeds the committee

### The divergence, recorded rather than swapped

§5A.5 says `round_randomness = drand.round(committee_time)`. This network does
not read drand: `genesis.js:52` is `RANDOMNESS_SOURCE = 'bitcoin-block-hash'`,
and 27 made `beaconIsAfterRound` refuse any round naming a rule that is not the
network's own. That is a signed-shape divergence of the same family as the
three on letter 15, and it is written down here rather than quietly reversed.

It has a consequence, which is this slice. `drand.round(committee_time)` names
a beacon BY TIME, so every node lands on one value without anybody naming it.
`bitcoin-block-hash` is only a SOURCE. Two honest nodes polling at different
moments take different tips, derive different seeds and seat different
committees. The selection rule is the missing half.

### The three picks, as implemented

    which block   the first whose median time past (BIP-113) is after
                  committee_time
    how deep      the round's own censusConfirmations - one confirmation
                  policy for chain-derived facts, not a second constant
    the height    derived from committee_time and the chain, never read from
                  the contract, because an author who names the height picks
                  the block and picking the block is grinding

ONE CORRECTION TO THE INSTRUCTION, and it is not a liberty. The pick said "at
or after committee_time"; the rule selects STRICTLY after. 27 already refuses a
beacon AT committee_time - the creator could have held it when the round was
made - so selecting a block at that instant would hand the validator a block it
must reject. Selection and validation have to agree and the stricter one wins.
The mutant that changes `>` to `>=` takes 4 tests red, so the boundary is held
rather than assumed.

MEDIAN TIME PAST IS ELEVEN INCLUDING ITSELF. Bitcoin Core's
`GetMedianTimePast` walks back eleven entries starting at the block, so it is
heights N-10..N. Eleven-with-itself and eleven-before-it are different numbers
on the same chain, so it is written out.

THE VIEW IS HEADERS, NOT BLOCKS. 25.1's providers serve 80-byte headers and
`agreedChain` weighs those; a beacon needs a hash and a time, and neither is in
a transaction. Asking for whole blocks would demand of a provider something the
protocol never asks it for. Mined and linked are still checked, by `chainWork`,
which is the same function the work comparison uses.

### Measured

A fifteen-block fixture from height 100, ten minutes apart, with
committee_time set exactly at the median of height 111:

    the first block whose MTP is after committee_time   112   (not 111, not the tip)
    its hash                    the hash of that header, not the tip's
    its depth against tip 114   3
    two views of the same chain same height, same hash, same committee seed
    censusConfirmations 4       refused: "is 3 deep and this round asks for 4",
                                and one more block makes the same choice settled
    committee_time far ahead    refused: "no block in this view is after this
                                round's committee time ..."
    a nine-block view           refused: "9 blocks and a median time past is
                                taken over 11"
    beaconHeight/height/randomnessHeight/beacon on the contract
                                changes nothing - the chosen height is the same

A LYING TIMESTAMP MOVES THE CHOICE BY ONE BLOCK, NOT BY SIX, and the first
version of this test asserted it moved the choice by NONE, which was wrong.
With one header two hours ahead:

    against the header's own nTime   the choice would be height 106
    against the median              111 instead of 112

So the median BOUNDS a miner's influence rather than removing it: moving it
further takes six of the eleven, and even then a miner picks a height and not a
hash. The depth rule is the other half - by the time a seed is deep enough to
use, moving it means re-mining that many blocks. Named here rather than left
for somebody to discover.

### Mutants

    takes the last qualifying block instead of the first     5 tests red
    reads the header time instead of the median             4 tests red
    no depth check                                          1 test red
    at-or-after instead of after                            4 tests red
    reads a height off the contract when one is present     1 test red

reader. It DECIDES NOTHING - no tip preference, no widening window, no cached
answer - it fetches 80-byte headers over RPC and hands them to

## Item 32, slice 3: the 2-of-2 tool no longer invents a seed

`round-2of2.mjs` answered every beacon question with
`{ hash: 32 x 0xbe, height: 900005, timeMs: 900n }`. It is gone. Given a
bitcoind (RT= and RPCPORT=), the beacon is the block the chain names; given
none, `randomnessFor` is not passed at all and the daemons' own defaults answer
nothing, which 27 turns into "this node has no beacon for that round, so it
cannot say who the census seats".

### What that constant actually was, measured

It was not seating anybody. The tool's `committee_time` became `Date.now()` in
slice 2 of letter 28, and 27 refuses a beacon at or before that instant:

    seed from 32 x 0xbe   "that randomness is from 900, at or before this
                           round's committee time 1788910693000 - the creator
                           could have held it when the round was made"
    seed from the chain    d964a1b2a7c2397d82479f0bc741cbb0277e6b95576ec89acc4fa0a1ea3959c8

So what is replaced is not a working stub but a misleading one: a source that
looked like an answer and was refused downstream. The tool now either holds a
real block or says it holds none.

### The synchronous question and the asynchronous chain

`roster.seedFor` asks for the beacon in the middle of seating and reading a
chain is a fetch, so `beacon-source.js` reads AHEAD of the question and holds
what the rule decided.

HOLDING THE ANSWER IS SAFE AND HOLDING THE TIP WOULD NOT BE, and the difference
is the whole reason it is allowed: for a given `committee_time`, the first
block whose median time is after it does not change as the chain grows. A later
read finds the same block DEEPER, not a different block. A reorg is the one
thing that could move it, which is what the depth requirement is for.

## M3 slice 1, the baseline: three rules about a stake, and nobody runs them

Printed rather than assumed, before a line of Lightning is written.

    settlementAction     23.2's table, per entry            1 caller (slash.js:546)
    holdSettlement       the whole round's settle/cancel    0 callers
    holdAfter            what state a hold ends in          0 callers
    invoiceMatchesEntry  should a player pay this invoice   0 callers

Three of the four are called only by their own tests - 3, 2 and 1 test files
respectively - and by nothing in any `src` or `tools`. The chapter's decisions
are written and none of them decides anything yet, which is the fifth time this
session a correct rule turned out to be constructed by nobody: GhostField,
checkHandout, the verifier's committee seed, beaconIsTheChains, and now the
whole stake table.

WHAT A NODE DOES AT CLOSE TODAY. `replay.js:193` maps the core's own outcome to
section 13's `result`: RUN_DELIVERED becomes DELIVERED and anything else that
ended becomes FAILED, with FORFEIT, VOID and ENTRY_VOID named as NOT reachable
from a replay. Nothing downstream of that touches money: `server.js:108` says
in as many words that "a stake is a hold invoice on Lightning and there is no
payment layer here yet", and the daemon's whole answer to funding is to refuse
unless an operator says otherwise.

    grep for addholdinvoice / settleinvoice / cancelinvoice / lnd / lightning
    across every src and tools file:  0 hits that are not a comment

So the starting number for this slice is zero callers and zero invoices, and
the property to protect is already written down in `payout.js`: a VOID EXPIRES
rather than being cancelled, "a cancel is an ACT, and it needs five of seven; a
refund that needed an act is one an operator could withhold".

### SINGLE-NODE CUSTODY, NOT §23.5

Named in those words on Daniel's ruling, so nobody reads a threshold into this
slice that is not there. This machine has one LND (`lnd v0.21.3-beta`), and the
2-of-2 has two daemons: one is the custodian and the other is not. §23.5 wants
every operation on the pool to need 5-of-7, and §23.6 wants the settlement
committee's own endpoint to issue the invoice. Neither is true here. What this
slice buys is the state machine - held, settled, cancelled, expired - driven by
the core's outcome, on worthless regtest coins. FROST closes the custody gap;
this does not, and does not pretend to.

### M3 STEP 2 — THE INJECTED CUSTODY PORT, AND WHAT THE FOUR OUTCOMES DO

`blwp-node/src/custody.js`. The port has the four operations Daniel named -
`createHeld`, `look`, `settle`, `cancel` - and it is injected exactly the way
`sign`, the curve, `chainFor` and `randomnessFor` are: the protocol decides,
the transport is handed in. The suite uses a fake port that keeps a call log
and no money, so all of this is measured with no Lightning node running at all.

CALLERS, BEFORE AND AFTER. The whole point of the step-1 baseline:

    settlementAction     1 caller  (slash.js:546)      ->  1  (unchanged)
    holdSettlement       0 callers                     ->  1  (custody.js:117)
    holdAfter            0 callers                     ->  1  (custody.js:137)
    invoiceMatchesEntry  0 callers                     ->  1  (custody.js:106)

    create on seat        one createHeld per entry, against the entry's own
                          stakeCommitment and stakeMsat - never an argument
    held while live       state HELD, "in nobody's balance"; asked twice, one
                          invoice (a second would be a second claim on one stake)
    DELIVERED             CANCELLED - one cancel call, the stake returns
    FORFEIT               SETTLED   - one settle call, the stake enters the pool
    VOID                  EXPIRED   - ZERO port calls of any kind

The VOID row is the one that matters. It is asserted as an absence: the void
player's payment hash appears in no `settle` and no `cancel` in the port's log.
23.2 says the HTLC expires and the wallet is refunded automatically, and a
cancel is an act an operator could withhold.

answer for stays HELD with zero port calls - not a refusal, because a hold
nobody may act on expires back to its payer on its own. That is step 3's
property arriving early: not acting is safe, acting early is not.

### M3 STEP 3 — KILL THE CUSTODIAN AND SEE WHO GOT PAID

`blwp-node/tools/custody-crash.mjs`. Not a unit test: a child process with a

A REPEATED SETTLE IS A SECOND PREIMAGE RELEASE. That is the measurement's whole
value - it was not a suspicion, it was printed - and it is the reason the
kill happens where it happens.

THE FIX IS THE INTENT ON DISK BEFORE THE CALL, not after: a hold goes to
`ACTING` first, which is the one state in `custody.js` that is not 23.2's. It
does not say what happened to the stake; it says something may have. A close
that finds one refuses to act on it and says so by name.

THE FOURTH PORT OPERATION IS WHAT RESOLVES IT. `look` had no caller until now.
`reconcile({roundId})` asks Lightning about every `ACTING` stake and writes the
answer down, because the node holding the preimage is the only party that knows:

    Lightning says SETTLED    the act landed; the stake moved, and will not
                              be settled twice
    Lightning says HELD       the act never left; the stake is HELD again and
                              the next close makes it once
    a port with no `look`     REFUSED - an interrupted act stays ACTING rather
                              than being resolved by guessing
    an answer that is not a
    state a hold can be in    REFUSED, by name

After the fix, the same crash re-run:

    lightning was told to settle 1 stake
    this node's store said                  ACTING
    reconciled against Lightning            1 -> SETTLED
    the whole log after the restart         2 settle calls, 0 repeated

### M3 STEP 4 — THE SAME RULES AGAINST `lnd v0.21.3-beta`

`blwp-node/src/lnd-port.js` is the transport; `blwp-node/tools/custody-lnd.mjs`
starts an isolated regtest of its own - own bitcoind datadir, non-default ports
(29643/29644, zmq on 29745/29746, lnd on 29650 and 29660), cookie auth - runs
one round on it, and stops every process when the numbers are in. No mainnet or
testnet4 datadir is opened, and `/mnt/bitcoin` is read for the two binaries and
nothing else.

TWO LND NODES, BECAUSE A HOLD CANNOT BE SETTLED UNTIL SOMEBODY HAS PAID IT.
Alice is the player's wallet; Bob is the daemon's custodian. Alice's three
payments sit in flight while Bob decides what the core's outcome word means.

    channel active                 alice 996530000 msat, bob 1000000000
    three stakes in flight         alice 996230000        (300000 msat out)
    lnd says ACCEPTED x3, this node says HELD x3

    winner   DELIVERED  -> CANCEL   -> CANCELLED
    loser    FORFEIT    -> SETTLE   -> SETTLED
    voided   VOID       -> NOTHING  -> EXPIRED

    after the acts                 alice 996330000, bob 1000100000
    the pool gained                100000 msat, one forfeited stake

THE THIRD ROW IS THE ONE WORTH THE WAIT, and what refunds the player was
measured rather than assumed. The first run set a 90-second invoice expiry and
waited 150 seconds: the stake was still held. AN INVOICE EXPIRY STOPS APPLYING
THE MOMENT AN HTLC IS ACCEPTED. What refunds a player when nobody acts is
BITCOIN'S timelock, in blocks:

    the void HTLC expires at height 345, the chain was at 262
    nobody acted; the tool mined
    at height 332 lnd failed it back  (13 blocks early - lnd's broadcast delta)
    alice's payment FAILED and her balance went back to 996430000 msat

So "the HTLC expires and the wallet is refunded automatically" is a consensus
rule and not a courtesy, which is exactly the property the chapter leans on -
and the tool mines rather than sleeps now.

    alice is down    100000 msat   exactly the forfeited stake
    bob is up        100000 msat   and nobody is keeping a difference

A SETTLE TAKES THE PREIMAGE, NOT THE HASH. `lncli settleinvoice` wants the 32
bytes, because releasing them IS the settlement - which is why 23.4 asks for
five of seven preimage shares first. `Custody` therefore takes an injected
`preimageFor`, and:

    no preimage             the stake stays HELD and expires to its player;
                            not being able to settle is not a loss
    a preimage that is not
    the one the hold was
    made for                REFUSED by name, before the port is called

`preimageFor` is the named gap letter 29's Feldman handouts close: reconstruct
from five shares and hand back 32 bytes. The tool supplies them directly.

LND'S WORDS ARE NOT 23.2'S, mapped in `lnd-port.js` and nowhere else. OPEN and
ACCEPTED are both HELD - money in flight is in nobody's balance whether or not
the player has paid yet. lnd has no word for a hold that timed out and calls it
CANCELED, so this node's own row is the only place EXPIRED is recorded, which
is what the last line of the tool's output says.

THE ONE-DOOR RULE HELD, and it took a real attempt to weaken it: `custody.js`
imported `sha256bytes` from `core/src/sha256.js` for a stake commitment, and
`round.test.js`'s audit failed immediately with

    + 'custody.js'
      'replay.js'

for exactly the reason its own comment predicted - "one more import, in one
more place, for one good reason". A hash is not a simulation, so `sha256` is
named in `protocol/src/hash.js` and the node takes it from there.

MUTATION, 20 mutants against 18 tests (14 custody, 4 port): 18 killed, the same
2 retracted as equivalent. The three new ones all died: settling with no
preimage at all, accepting any 32 bytes as one, and not handing it to the port.

STILL SINGLE-NODE CUSTODY, NOT §23.5. Bob is one node holding everyone's money,
with one macaroon an operator could use by hand. FROST closes that; this does
not.

A STRANGER'S ENTRY IS REFUSED, and the refusal is the honest one: this node
does not invent invoices for entries it never seated (404). It cannot mean "not

stranger holding it can only fund that player's stake, never take it.

THE MEASUREMENT THAT CHANGED THE CODE. Closing a real round on the daemon

### M3.3-9 STEP 1 — WHO CAN OPEN A STAKE TODAY

Printed before a line of this item is written, the way the hold-invoice
baseline was - and this time the caller count is the FIRST thing measured, not
the thing that was assumed.

THE ARITHMETIC IS ALL THERE AND NOTHING RUNS IT. `packages/protocol/src/shares.js`,
callers outside its own file and its own tests:

    splitSecret         who cuts the polynomial            0
    reconstruct         five shares back to 32 bytes       0
    openStake           and does it hash to the stake      0
    shareIsConsistent   one share against the commitments  0
    handoutOutcome      what a handout amounts to          0
    checkHandout        the crooked-dealer door            2   (letter 29)

The four grep hits for "reconstruct" outside `shares.js` are all COMMENTS. So
letter 29 built the door and the arithmetic, and the only thing in the system
that ever produced 32 bytes for a settle is `tools/custody-lnd.mjs`, which
hands them over directly. `serve()`'s `preimageFor` defaults to null, so a
shipped daemon settles nothing at all.

AND THE SHARES ARE IN THE CLEAR, which `handout.js` says about itself: "anybody
who reads a handout reads five shares and rebuilds P... It becomes REQUIRED at
the same moment the hold invoice does... A build that pays sats must not use
this file as it stands." The hold invoice went live at c545c36. Measured
against a running daemon, by a stranger holding nothing but the public
`vss_shares_ref` that the entry contract carries:

    POST /handout                                   201
    GET  /handout?id=      shares a stranger reads    7
    subsets of 5 that open the stake                 21 of 21
    the stranger reconstructed the preimage          true
    and it hashes to the entry's stakeCommitment     true

So today the answer to "who holds the 32 bytes" is EVERYONE. Reconstruction
from five of seven, added on top of this, would change nothing: one node
settles alone and so does a passer-by. Encrypting one share to each seat is not
a refinement of this item, it is the item.

NOBODY DEALS EITHER. `blwp-client/src/join.js:213` sets
`stakeCommitment: random(32)` - a commitment to nothing, not `sha256(P)` - and
`vssSharesRef: NO_SHARES`. Letter 29 wrote that "the page is not a dealer,
which arrives with the hold invoice". It has arrived.

AND THERE IS NO WAY FOR SEATS TO ASK EACH OTHER. Seventeen routes and none of
them carries a share; `gather` fetches `/results` from peers and there is no
equivalent. Once a seat holds only its own share, five can never meet.

THE THREE MEASURES THIS ITEM CLOSES ON: a stranger opens ZERO shares, four
answers refuse by name, five reconstruct and hash to that entry's own
stakeCommitment. All three are false today - 7, opens, opens.

### M3.3-9 STEP 2 — ONE SHARE, ONE SEAT, AND NOBODY ELSE

`packages/protocol/src/seal.js` is the missing half of 23.1 step 2 - "encrypts
one share to each settlement-committee member" - and `handout.js` now carries
envelopes instead of scalars.

THE PICK, as ruled: ECDH on the curve this system already injects, then AES-GCM
through WebCrypto. No new dependency: `@noble/ciphers` is not vendored and does
not need to be, and both ends of this - a browser dealing and a daemon opening -
already have `crypto.subtle`.

    key    taggedHash(BLWP/v1/VssShareKey,   ecdh(x) || seat)
    nonce  taggedHash(BLWP/v1/VssShareNonce, ecdh(x) || seat)[0..12]
    seal   AES-GCM over the 32-byte scalar   -> 48 bytes with the tag

TWO TAGS AND NOT ONE, because a key and a nonce derived from the same bytes
under one tag would BE the same bytes. THE NONCE IS DERIVED, NOT DRAWN: a
random nonce would travel on the wire and make the handout - and therefore its
id, and therefore the `vss_shares_ref` inside a SIGNED entry - different on
every re-encode of one deal.

THE EVEN-Y NORMALISATION IS THE SUBTLETY, and it is measured rather than
argued. An x-only key names the point with even y, so a secret whose own point
has odd y is negated before multiplying, exactly as BIP-340 signing does:

    both ends derive the same secret       32 of 32 key pairs
    two different pairs derive one secret   0 of 32

WHAT MOVED, in the numbers this item closes on:

                                        before      after
    shares a stranger can read              7           7   (the wire is public)
    shares a stranger can OPEN              7           0
    five-subsets that open the stake       21 of 21     0
    a stranger reconstructs the preimage  true       false
    a seat opens its own share              -           7 of 7 seats
    a seat opens somebody else's            -           0 of 42 attempts

The refusal is by name, because GCM authenticates: a wrong key does not decrypt
to a garbage scalar that then fails the Feldman check, it does not decrypt at
all - "seat N's share does not open under this key: it was sealed to somebody
else".

WHO CATCHES A CROOKED DEALER CHANGED, and that is worth stating plainly. A node
holds one share now, so it refuses when IT is the one cheated:

    seats that refused a dealer who cheated seat 5    1 of 7  (seat 5)
    seats that accepted                                6 of 7

That is not weaker than letter 29. A handout five seats accepted is a handout
five seats can open, which is the only property 5-of-7 needs; and a dealer who
cheats enough seats to break reconstruction is refused by every one of them.
What is gone is one seat catching a cheat aimed at another - it cannot see it,
which is the point.

A NODE THAT WAS DEALT NOTHING KEEPS NOTHING: `/handout` refuses with "this node
is not one of the seats that handout was dealt to" rather than storing an
envelope addressed to somebody else and calling it custody.

AND THE OPENED SHARE IS NEVER WRITTEN DOWN. Only the sealed handout goes to
disk and the share is re-opened from it when needed, so a stolen database is a
pile of envelopes. The `holds` table gained nothing.

### M3.3-9 STEP 2b — THE PAGE DEALS

Letter 29 named it: "the page is not a dealer, which arrives with the hold
invoice". It arrived. Measured before: `join.js:213` set

anywhere in the system - and `vssSharesRef: NO_SHARES`.

`stakeFor(round, { seats, curve, random, playerPubkey })` now does 23.1 steps 1
and 2 in the page: choose P, publish `sha256(P)`, split it 5-of-7 over the
settlement committee, seal one share to each seat, and hand back the handout to
POST. P never leaves the page.

    stakeCommitment === sha256(preimage)        true   (was: random bytes)
    vssSharesRef === handoutId(handout)         true   (was: 32 zero bytes)
    seats that open their own share             7 of 7

THE CURVE IS INJECTED, exactly like `sign` and `verify`. `bundle.js` says why:
"a vendored curve would be an implementation of the thing that pins money,
sitting in the page, that nobody audits." So the page hands in
`pointFromScalar`, `combinePoints`, `ecdhShared` and `pointX`, and the bundle
still carries no crypto - it grew from 25 to 27 modules and none of them is a
curve.

AND IT IS AN INPUT DEVICE. Nothing in `stakeFor` computes an outcome, reads a
truck or decides what a run came to. It generates key material and encodes it.

P IS NOT REDUCED. `splitSecret` refuses a preimage at or above the group order
rather than taking it modulo n, because reducing would change the number the
payment hash already commits to; `stakeFor` draws another instead.

THE BUNDLE CHANGED, for the first time in this slice: 277.2 KB from 27 modules,
and the WebGL template's copy was re-synced, because a template that ships a
different client from the one the suites measure is a page running a different
program.

### M3.3-10 STEP 1 — WHO CAN MOVE THE POOL TODAY, AND THE VECTORS TO MEASURE AGAINST

Printed before a line of FROST is written.

THERE IS NO POOL WALLET. `payout.js` names one twice - "the stake enters the
pool wallet" - and nothing in this repo holds one. Settled stakes land in
whatever Lightning node `lndPort` was pointed at, and `lnd-port.js` says what
that means in its own header: "one `lncli`, one macaroon, one operator who
could run every one of these commands by hand."

    keys that must agree before a satoshi leaves the pool     1
    FROST code in packages/*/src                             0 files
                                                             3 grep hits, ALL prose
    RFC 9591 vectors reproduced                              0 of 0 - no test file
    a 4-of-7 attempt                                         no such thing to refuse

AND `aggregateKeys` IS NOT A THRESHOLD, checked rather than assumed. It is
BIP-327 MuSig2 key aggregation for the bond key path (5A.3B), and MuSig2 needs
EVERY signer. It cannot express five of seven and is not going to be dressed up
as though it can. It also has no caller outside `bond-script.js`.

WHAT §23.5 ACTUALLY ASKS FOR: "Settled loser stakes accumulate in a wallet
whose every operation requires a 5-of-7 threshold signature of the settlement
committee. No node and no minority can move a satoshi, at any moment, including
during payout."

THE VECTORS ARE FETCHED, NOT TYPED. `test-vectors/protocol/rfc9591-secp256k1.json`
was extracted mechanically from the RFC text - no hex was retyped:

    source        https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9591.txt
    sha256        928d0142da7c30f6e4acab8164dd5d610cc52381ba348e229d7ce7f2f567ae30
    section       E.5.  FROST(secp256k1, SHA-256)
    fields        30, wrapped hex re-joined by the extractor
    config        MAX 3, MIN 2, NUM 2; signers 1 and 3
    signature     65 bytes (33-byte R element || 32-byte scalar)

TWO CIPHERSUITES, IN ORDER, AND THE REASON. RFC 9591's secp256k1 suite is NOT
BIP-340: it hashes a different challenge, serialises R as a 33-byte compressed
point rather than 32 x-only bytes, and has no even-y rule. Those vectors prove
the ALGEBRA - Lagrange interpolation over the signer set, binding factors,
share aggregation - and Bitcoin will not verify a signature they produce. So
the RFC suite is measured first because it is the only thing with published
numbers, and then the BIP-340 variant is measured the only way that matters:
`schnorr.verify` accepts a 5-of-7 signature against one 32-byte key.

### M3.3-10 STEP 2 — THE RFC'S OWN NUMBERS, THEN THE ONE BITCOIN CHECKS

`packages/protocol/src/frost.js` is RFC 9591 with the curve injected, and every
number below is the RFC's rather than this implementation's opinion of itself.
Appendix E.5, FROST(secp256k1, SHA-256), reproduced byte for byte:

    the trusted dealer's three shares          3 of 3
    the group public key                       matches
    both nonces of both signers, from the
    RFC's own randomness                       4 of 4
    the nonce commitments                      4 of 4
    the binding factor INPUTS (129 bytes each) 2 of 2
    the binding factors                        2 of 2
    the signature shares                       2 of 2
    the aggregate signature (65 bytes)         matches
    Appendix B's own check on it               g^z is R + PK*c

    RFC 9591 vectors reproduced                0 of 9  ->  9 of 9

expand_message_xmd is written out rather than imported, because this package
carries no hashing library either - `sha256` comes from the core the way every
other hash here does, and the rest is byte plumbing. L is 48 and not 32: the
extra 128 bits are what make the reduction's bias unexploitable, and a mutant
setting it to 32 died against the vectors.

### AND THEN THE SIGNATURE A TAPROOT OUTPUT CAN CHECK

RFC 9591's secp256k1 suite is NOT BIP-340 - its own challenge tag, a 33-byte
compressed R, no even-y rule - so nothing on the Bitcoin network would verify
what it produces. `frost-bip340.js` is the same threshold over BIP-340's
conventions, and THE VERIFIER IS NOT OURS: `schnorr.verify`, the one a taproot
spend gets.

    a 5-of-7 signature BIP-340 accepts         8 of 8 dealings, 64 bytes each
    any five of the seven, same key            4 of 4 signing sets
    four of seven, refused by name             "4 of 5 signers: a pool nobody
                                               can move stays where it is"
    four of seven that sign anyway             0 of 3 accepted
    ONE NODE ALONE                             0 of 7 accepted
    the same signature over another message    refused
    a share from another dealing               refused

    keys that must agree before a satoshi
    leaves the pool                            1  ->  5 of 7

TWO PARITY FIXES AND ONLY ONE AT SIGNING TIME. The group key is normalised when
it is dealt, so P is even and stays even. R cannot be - it depends on whoever
turned up - so every signer reads its parity off the public commitment list and
negates its own nonces when it is odd. Measured rather than argued: over 24
signatures the group commitment came out odd 4 to 20 times (a coin), and 24 of
24 verified. A mutant deleting the flip killed four tests.

### M3.3-13 STEPS 3 TO 5 — THE POOL IS A KEY, AND CONSENSUS TOOK THE SPEND

SO THE TWEAK COMMITS TO NOTHING, which is BIP-341's own instruction for a
key-path-only output: Q = P + H_TapTweak(P)*G with an empty merkle root.
Skipping it would also spend, but it would publish a raw group key and every
taproot reader would ask what tree it was hiding.

WHAT A SIGNER DOES ABOUT THE TWEAK IS TWO ADDITIONS AND NO NEW PROTOCOL. Adding
the same constant to every share adds it to the secret, because the
interpolating values sum to one over any signing set; negating every share
negates it. Both measured rather than argued - a committee that skipped the
tweak holds shares of the INTERNAL key, which no output pays to, and its
signature verifies against nothing.

### M3.3-16 — THE RELAY FLOOR IS PER ROW, AND THE SHORTFALL IS A DEBT

THE NUMBER THE NODE ACTUALLY HOLDS, asked of a fresh isolated regtest rather
than remembered or derived:

    minrelaytxfee                     0.00000100 BTC/kvB
    a P2TR output of 329 sats         "Transaction amount too small"
    a P2TR output of 330 sats         accepted, txid returned

An arithmetic derivation from the dust-relay formula gave 796 and was WRONG.
The node's own boundary is the number, so `DUST_SATS = 330n` stands as a
DEFAULT a caller overrides with what their chain said - and the regtest tool
now asks the chain for it by offering one sat at a time from 300 up, rather
than trusting the constant.

WHAT THE CODE DID BEFORE, instrumented at named amounts through
`payoutOutputs`:

    owed    1 sat     refused, whole round
    owed  329 sats    refused, whole round
    owed  330 sats    paid
    owed  545 sats    paid
    owed  331 sats    paid

    one row of 5000 sats beside one row of 100    THE WHOLE ROUND REFUSED

So a sub-dust OUTPUT was already impossible - the fault was the opposite of
what item 16's line assumed: one player owed 100 sats stopped a player owed
5000 from being paid at all. That is the number that moved.

    a 5000-sat winner beside a 100-sat one   0 outputs  ->  1 output, 5000 paid
    a 5000 + 700 + 100 round                 0 outputs  ->  2 outputs, 5700 paid
    the 100 sats                             lost in a refusal -> recorded as owed

THE RULE, AND THE THREE THINGS IT REFUSES TO DO. Rows at or above the floor are
paid; rows below it are left owed, named, and returned to the caller, which
writes the debt on the round. The sats are:

    not bumped to the floor   that pays a player out of other players' winnings
    not folded into the fee   the miner is not who the round owes
    not dropped              dropping is the operator keeping money a player
                             had no part in losing

They stay in the pool with the debt recorded, and the round is NOT `PAID` while
they are there - it is `PAID_IN_PART`. A round where nobody clears the floor
builds no transaction at all and keeps the debt.

    payouts.owed_sats / owed_count   round-scoped, on the row that already
                                     exists. A balance that accumulates ACROSS
                                     rounds is a policy this letter does not
                                     invent, and neither is a Lightning payout.

ON A REAL CHAIN, isolated regtest, own datadir, ports 29673/29674, cookie auth,
stopped and removed:

    the floor this node enforces      330 sats, asked of it directly
    five of seven                     sendrawtransaction -> txid, block 202
    the winner's own key holds        1000 sats
    the round's row                   PAID, owes 0 sats to 0 players
    a winner owed 329 sats            NOT SENT: "there is no output to make"
    that round's row                  329 sats owed to 1 player, PAYOUT_QUEUED

MUTATION: 9 mutants against the floor and the debt, ALL 9 KILLED, nothing
retracted. Dropping a sub-floor row, bumping it to the floor, ignoring the
floor, building a spend when nobody clears it, hiding the owed rows from the
answer, calling a short round PAID, and clearing the debt on a later state
write all died. The last one needed a new test rather than a retraction:
`putPayout` is called again for every transition and none of those callers
knows the debt, so a write that reset it would quietly clear what a round owes
on its way to being marked paid.

WHAT THIS DOES NOT DO, and it is on the list rather than here: the sats are
owed and there is still nothing that pays them. That needs either a balance
carried across rounds until it clears the floor, or a Lightning payout - and
the second would make the pool something other than the taproot output item 13
proved.

  the heading dropped (identity rotation)    -> faces somewhere its ints never pointed
  the heading divided like a metre           -> faces somewhere its ints never pointed
    (16384/65536 = 0.25 deg for a quarter turn - the M1 fault, pinned again)
  a truck placed once and never moved again  -> not at the x its ints name
  the clone left inactive                    -> not active, so nobody sees it
The last one is why the test asks `activeInHierarchy` and not `renderer.enabled`:
an inactive clone HAS an enabled renderer and is on nobody's screen.

## M3.3 item 17: what a payout signature costs today, measured before anything is written

The 8b row names it: "one process still holds five shares, and a real payout
needs a signing round between daemons". Measured rather than assumed:

  - `Payouts#pay` takes `signers`, an array of `{ id, share }`. `share` is a
    SECRET scalar. `test/payout-pay.test.js` hands it `dealt.shares.slice(0, 5)`
    straight off `trustedDealerSplit`, so five secrets are in one process, and
    that process generates all ten nonces and all five signature shares in one
    `map`. Five of seven is arithmetic there, not a threshold: whoever runs that
    map can sign anything.
  - CALLERS OF `pay` OUTSIDE TESTS: zero. `grep -rn "\.pay(" src/` finds
    nothing. The same shape FROST had when it landed.
  - THE DAEMON HOLDS NO SHARE. `serve` takes `poolKey` and passes it to
    `Payouts` as `pool`; it defaults to null and NOTHING in `src/` or
    `src/main.js` ever sets it. There is no seat share anywhere in the daemon.
  - NO DOOR CARRIES A SIGNATURE. The 21 doors `server.js` answers are the
    census, the round, the entry, the transcript, the receipts, the results,
    the objection, the committee, the invoice, the handout and `/share` - which
    is 29's VSS share of the STAKE PREIMAGE, a different secret for a different
    purpose. Nothing serves a nonce commitment and nothing serves a signature
    share.

So the number of keys that must agree before a settled satoshi moves is still
ONE - the process that calls `pay`. 13 moved it off a single Lightning macaroon
and onto a group key; it did not move it onto a group.

WHAT THE LETTER HAS TO BE, and what it must not quietly become: a dealerless
DKG is its own letter (the FROST row says so) and this is not it. The seats are
still dealt their shares. What changes is that a share never leaves the seat
that holds it, and that a seat signs only a spend IT built from the round's own
final table - a seat that signed whatever sighash it was handed would make the
threshold decorative, because five signatures over an attacker's transaction
spend the pool exactly as well as five over a real one.

## M3.3 item 17, built: a signing round between daemons, and a chain that took it

The measurement above said the number of keys that had to agree before a
settled satoshi moved was ONE - the process that ran `pay`'s `map` over five
secret shares. It is five now, on five sockets.

TWO DOORS, both fixed-width so a stranger can read them and neither carrying a
sighash:

    POST /pool/commit?round=  <- one output (78 bytes)        -> one commitment
    POST /pool/share?round=   <- that output + the list       -> one scalar

THE RULE UNDERNEATH is that a seat signs only a spend IT built. The obvious
door takes a sighash and returns a share, and it is worth nothing: five
signatures over an attacker's 32 bytes spend the pool exactly as well as five
over a real payout, so a committee that signs what it is handed has a threshold
on paper and one key in practice. The asker names the round and the OUTPUT it
wants spent - both facts anybody can check - and every seat rebuilds the rest
from its own store: its own results, its own entries, its own table, §20's five
of seven over that table, the pool's own script, and only then a sighash it
computed for itself.

NONCES IN MEMORY, ON PURPOSE. Two messages under one nonce pair is two
equations in two unknowns and publishes the share. A pair that is never written
down cannot come back after a restart to be used again - a restart costs the
asker a seat and it asks another. While the process lives the pair remembers
which message it was made for: a retry gets the SAME commitment and the SAME
share back, a different spend is refused while a pair is live, and a different
COMMITMENT LIST over the same spend is refused too, because the list is hashed
into the binding factors and therefore into the challenge.

ON A REAL CHAIN (`tools/payout-committee-regtest.mjs`), seven daemons on seven
sockets, one share each, isolated regtest:

    a rogue asker naming its own output   7 of 7 seats REFUSED, 409, by name
    four of seven                          nothing sent, row stays PAYOUT_QUEUED
    five of seven                          sendrawtransaction -> a txid,
                                           block 202 carries it, the winner's
                                           own key holds 1000 sats, the asker's
                                           store says PAID signed by 5 seats

THE ROGUE LINE IS THE LETTER. There is no door that takes a sighash, so the
attack an asker would want has no shape; the nearest it can do is name an
output of its own, and seven seats say no with a sentence each.

THE FAULT THAT MATTERED was in the injection and not the crypto. The daemon
built its `Payouts` with `fetcher: (u) => fetch(u)`, which drops the second
argument, so every POST to a peer left as a GET and came back "no such door".
The first run had one of five seats committing - the local one. A fetcher that
silently changes the method of every request it forwards is the kind of thing
only a real socket finds.

AND ONE FOUND BY ITS OWN TEST: `poolOwns` answers with an object, so
`if (!poolOwns(...))` is always false. The check that stops a seat signing a
spend of anybody's coin never fired.

MUTATION: 11 against it, 10 killed, ONE RETRACTED. `spendFor` also compared the
recomputed table id with the one on the payout row. No test could tell that
check on from off, and the reason is that it is not load-bearing: the
verification underneath asks the SEATS about the recomputed id, so a node whose
own results moved already fails with "0 of 5". The only state it caught was a
committee that had all moved to the same new table while this node's row was
stale, where refusing refuses a spend the committee agrees on.

  killed: the pool-ownership check skipped; a queued row standing in for five
  of seven; a retry given a fresh nonce pair; a second live pair allowed; a
  spent pair signing again under a new list; round two not checking what round
  one committed to; the seat not checking it is in the list; the seat not
  checking the list quotes its own commitment; the asker sending below the
  threshold; the wire half-reading a truncated commitment list.

WHAT IS NOT HERE, NAMED RATHER THAN ABSORBED:

  - `payWithCommittee` HAS NO CALLER IN `src/`. A close queues the payout and
    stops, because the daemon does not know WHICH OUTPUT holds the pool - there
    is no watcher for the pool's script and `chainSpend` can only `send` and
    `look`. The seat half is fully wired and any asker can reach it; the asking
    half needs an output to name. That is item 18 and it is its own line.
  - `pay` - the one-process path that takes five secret shares as an argument -
    is still in the file. It has zero callers in `src/` and nothing in the
    daemon can reach it; `payout-regtest.mjs` and `payout-pay.test.js` are what
    use it, and those legitimately hold the whole dealt pool. Removing it is
    tidying, not this letter.
  - The shares are still DEALT. A dealerless DKG is its own letter and this one
    does not pretend to be it.

## M2.36, after the 16:08 two-Chrome close-out: two faults, both named and both fixed

THE FIRST STOPPED THE PAGE FROM STARTING AT ALL. The Daily shipped
`script.src = 'Build/{{{ LOADER_FILENAME }}}'` - seven unfilled template tokens,
not one - so Unity never started and the page sat on its own loading screen
looking like a slow download. SwissClaw found it by injecting webgl5.loader.js
by hand. How it got there is not carelessness: the WebGL TEMPLATE is where the
page is edited, and an edit reaches a deploy by being copied over Unity's built
index.html, which brings the tokens back. `unity-proto/tools/fill-template.mjs`
fills them from the build that is there - four names read out of `Build/`, the
company/product/version out of ProjectSettings - and `--check` exits non-zero if
any is left. Both deploy scripts fill and then check before they upload, so an
unfilled page cannot reach Cloudflare again.

THE SECOND IS WHY THE GHOST FROZE, and the measurement came before the fix.

  - THE DAEMON PATH IS NOT THE FAULT. A watcher on a real socket was driven
    through 6000 published ticks in 40 batches and held the newest tick every
    single time: published through 149 -> holds 149, ... published through 5999
    -> holds 5999. Not one batch behind.
  - A GAP IS NOT POSSIBLE. `Round#batch` refuses a non-contiguous batch at
    intake - "expected tick N, got M" - so the stored ticks have no holes for a
    warm ghost run to refuse to step across.
  - THE CLIENT RETRIED THE SAME BATCH FOREVER. On a refusal the words went back
    at the head of the hold and nothing else changed, so the next `drain` built
    the identical batch. `nextTick` never moved again. Every watcher's picture
    of that truck stopped at the last tick that landed - 4241 - while the driver
    drove on, and from outside the run looked healthy: socket up, player count
    right, chip reading play · A up · 2 players.

THE FIX IS THAT A REFUSAL IS A DISAGREEMENT ABOUT WHERE THE RUN IS. The two
numbers that could be wrong - `nextTick` and `batchHead` - are re-read from the
node ONCE through `resume`, the same door a reconnect uses, which checks what it
is given rather than adopting it. A batch refused after that is not about the
numbers, and the run ends with the node's own words. A player whose inputs
nobody stores is not driving a round.

AND THE PAGE SAYS SO: `not publishing · <the node's own sentence>`, first on the
chip, above the count and the place, because it is the one fault none of the
other numbers can show.

MUTATION: 6 against it, 6 killed. Mutant 1 IS the behaviour this letter
replaces - "a refusal changes nothing" - and it fails two of the four tests,
which is what makes them a measurement rather than a description. Also killed:
resyncing on every refusal instead of once; ending without ever resyncing;
building a batch while the numbers are being re-read; a recovered run still
reporting a refusal; a chip with no line for it.

## M2.36, the 17:05 split: the two trucks were in two different worlds

MEASURED FIRST, on a real 2-of-2 round with two tabs joined the way the page
joins, before anything was changed:

    the seed the page gives its own core   0x5eed1234  bay 13  z  10.20 m
    the seed the committee replays with (left tab)     bay 20  z  57.80 m
    the seed the committee replays with (right tab)    bay 18  z  44.20 m

`CoreDrivenTruck.seed` is a CONSTANT - `public int seed = 0x5eed1234` - and
`grep` finds no assignment to it anywhere. So every player of every round
stepped their core in the harness world while the committee replayed each entry
with `seedWordForEntry(entry, randomness)`. That is not a bay offset: the seed
drives the whole rng stream after it, so the replayed truck is a different run
in a different world, which is why it "updates" and never matches. 17:05: a
ghost on the grass at -69,-57 m while the truck it pictured stood on its bay.

THE PAGE COULD NOT HAVE DONE BETTER. The seed is H(randomness || pubkey ||
world secret || join tick) and NOTHING SERVED THE RANDOMNESS - there was no
door for it. There is one now, `GET /randomness?round=`, serving the same value
the ghost replay uses, and the page asks EVERY node the URL named and refuses a
round where two of them name two worlds. That is not proof the hash is the
block 5A.5 names; deriving the height is letter 32's work and the page does not
do it, which is written down rather than implied.

THE ORDERING IS THE FIX, NOT A DETAIL. Every `BlwpStep` is published from the
moment there is a client - loading in the bay included, which is why the 16:08
report saw tick 4241 with the truck still on its apron - so a core reseeded at
roll-out would already have published thousands of ticks of the wrong world.
The bridge derives the seed and calls `init` BEFORE `net.client` exists, and
`net.tick` records nothing until it does. C# stopped throwing it away too:
`StartRound` restarted with its own constant and takes `BlwpNet.RoundSeed` now,
zero meaning the daily and the constant that holds the solo apron on bay 13.

THE END-TO-END TEST IS NOT CIRCULAR. One tab drives, the other is shown
pictures the daemon's own replay produced, and those are held against a core
the test steps itself in the seed `worldSeedFor` returns - and against a second
core in the harness world:

    the ghost the watcher was shown           (-99.437, 57.797) m at tick 47
    a core in the driver's own world          (-99.437, 57.797) m   delta 0
    a core in the harness world               (-99.437, 10.197) m   47.60 m away

x, z and heading to the word. The fixture DRAWS an identity whose world is not
the harness's, because one player in 24 lands on the solo bay by chance and a
fixture that agreed by accident every 24th run would be a test that passes on
the fault.

### The second fault, found by the test written for the first

A new PlayMode test hands the field the LOCAL truck's own core pose as somebody
else's picture and requires the ghost to be drawn where the local truck is
drawn. x and z matched to the millimetre. The HEIGHT did not, by 0.58 m: the
local truck at y 6.840 and a ghost at its own x, z and heading at 7.422, same
ground, same frame. The ghosts were seated on ONE ground sample under their
middle while a truck is fitted across its FOUR contact points. One rule now -
`CoreDrivenTruck.RideAt(x, z, heading)` - called by `Apply` and by the ghosts,
which is why `Seat` grew a heading: four points rotate and a centre sample does
not.

What that test asserts about height is not "the same y as the local truck", and
the difference is the Editor rather than the code: there is no core there, so
`Driving` is false and PhysX places the local truck. The claim is that a ghost
is seated by the same function a core-driven truck is seated by - which a y of
zero, a centre sample, or a dropped body offset all fail.

### The stutter, with its arithmetic

`BlwpNet.BatchEvery` is `TicksPerSecond / 10`. A picture lands at most ten times
a second; the page draws sixty times a second. `Show` placed the truck and left
it, so it stood still for six frames and jumped - 1.5 m at 15 m/s. The local
truck has never looked like that: `Apply` interpolates between its own last two
ticks every frame.

A ghost walks from its last picture onto its newest over one picture interval
and is then exactly on it. Measured: one frame after a 6.001 m picture it has
moved 0.112 m of it. `k` is clamped at one, so it never predicts - a ghost is a
picture (0.10) and an extrapolated one would be the page inventing somebody
else's position.

WRITTEN AS AN EXPONENTIAL FIRST, AND THAT WAS WRONG for a reason worth keeping:
an exponential never arrives, and how far it got depends on the FRAME RATE
rather than on the clock. A headless batch run puts frames a third of a
millisecond apart, and 600 of them closed a 6 m gap only to within 20 mm.
`Settled` was "within a millimetre" too, which is looser than the callers'
ten-thousandth of a metre - so a ghost could be settled and 0.3 mm short, and it
showed up as a red test that came and went with the frame rate. Arrival is the
end of the walk now, and `SnapToPicture` puts it exactly on the words.

## M2.36: what a live round reads of `CoreDrivenTruck.seed`, printed

The constant is still in the player - `public int seed = 0x5eed1234` - and a
constant that can put this player's core back in the harness world is the 17:05
fault waiting to happen again. So it was asked of the SHIPPED bridge rather
than of the source: `blwp.jslib` evaluated the way Emscripten evaluates it,
`$blwpDiscovery` included, driven against two real daemons, with every call
into the core's `init` logged and every `record` logged beside it
(`world-seed-bridge.test.js`).

    every init the shipped bridge asked the core for, in order:
      1. 0x5eed1234  bay 13  z 10.20 m   <- CoreDrivenTruck.seed, the constant
      2. 0x0ae8bebb  bay 16  z 30.60 m   <- the round
    ticks recorded before the round's init: 0
    BlwpRoundSeed() answers 0x0ae8bebb

THE TWO READ SITES, and what each one does on a live round:

  - `CoreDrivenTruck.Start`, line 112, `BlwpCore.Init(seed)`. READ, once, at
    scene start, before any round is joined. The truck steps in that world
    while the page is still discovering the chain and proving the bond - and
    NOTHING IS RECORDED out of it: `net.tick` returns at its first line while
    `net.client` is null, and the client is only assigned after `worldSeedFor`
    has resolved and `b.st = b.core.init(seedWord)` has replaced the state.
    Measured: 30 steps before the join, 0 records. The state that world
    produced is discarded, not published.
  - `CoreDrivenTruck.StartRound`, the roll-out. NOT READ on a live round: it
    takes `BlwpNet.RoundSeed`, which the bridge answers with the round's own
    seed. The constant is only the answer when that is zero, which is the daily.

No other reader. `grep` finds no assignment to the field anywhere, and the
scene serialises no override - `Bootstrap` adds the component at runtime.

### AND THE ROLL-OUT ITSELF WAS THE NEXT HOLE

`StartRound` restarted the core whatever world it named, and on a live round
that is wrong for a reason that has nothing to do with which seed it uses. The
run began when the page seeded the core, and the client has recorded every tick
since the join - the 16:08 report saw tick 4241 while the truck was still in its
bay. A restart in the middle puts the player's core back at tick zero while the
transcript they are publishing runs straight through. Measured, 120 ticks of one
drive with a roll-out at 60:

    the page holds   afa591f29d954df116434c4354c38496d825b4e72cf437c22e66048f87f5bd59
    the committee    686abbf1bb0bbc441a8187d18c76629d9c12aea95efb7e30fc7b008799f1f0d1
    z: page 30.589 m, committee 30.308 m

0.28 m apart after two seconds, and growing. Every mark the player signs after
it commits to a state nobody else computes, and every watcher's picture is of
the replay rather than of the truck being driven - the same class of fault as
the seed, by a different road.

`CoreDrivenTruck.RollOutRestarts(roundSeed, dailySeed, out world)` is the rule
now: the daily restarts into its constant, a live round is never restarted, and
a round whose own seed happens to BE the constant is still a round. Pure - no
core, no player - so `RollOutTests` measures it without one.

## M2.36: the two-Chrome look, for whoever runs it

Claude cannot run this. Everything below is what the page now claims, so that a
look either confirms it or names which claim is false.

STAND THE ROUND UP, then open the printed URL in TWO local Chrome windows -
real WebGL, not headless, not browser-act:

    node packages/blwp-node/tools/round-2of2.mjs

It prints one URL of the shape
`https://<page>/?round=<id>&node=<A>,<B>&bond=<A>/bond&advert=<hex>`. Both
windows get the SAME URL. Two tabs are two players because the key is per tab
(`sessionStorage`).

WHAT TO SEE, IN THIS ORDER:

  1. THE PAGE STARTS. If it sits on its own loading screen, look at the console
     for `Build/{{{ LOADER_FILENAME }}}` - that was the 16:08 fault and a deploy
     now refuses to ship it, so seeing it again means something bypassed
     `deploy-core.sh`.

  2. BEFORE EITHER TRUCK MOVES - this is the new one, and it is the whole
     letter. The two trucks must be on DIFFERENT loading bays, both on the
     apron at x about -100 m, and the console of each window says
     `[blwp] world seed 0x… from 2 node(s) agreeing on the round randomness`.
     Two nodes, not one. If either window says one, the page took a single
     daemon's word for which world it is in.
     Bays are 6.8 m apart and there are 24 of them, so the two z values can be
     anything from 6.8 m to 156 m apart. THEY MUST NOT BOTH BE 10.2 m: that is
     bay 13, the harness constant, and both trucks standing there is the old
     fault back.

  3. THE CHIPS MUST AGREE, IN METRES. Each window's chip carries
     `N players in this round · other at X,Z m` - that is where THAT window has
     drawn the OTHER truck. Hold each chip against the other window's own
     position readout:
       - same two numbers  -> the picture is right; if you cannot see the truck,
         the camera is pointed elsewhere, which is the bays being far apart and
         is not a fault
       - different numbers -> the picture is wrong, and the difference is the
         measurement to report
     At 17:05 they read `other at -69,-57 m` against a truck standing on the
     yellow bay - about 30 m out and 10 m across, in a world nobody replayed.

  4. ONE DRIVES PAST THE OTHER. Let P1 load and roll out; P2 stays in the bay
     and watches. P1's ghost in P2's window must FOLLOW - not appear at spawn
     and stop, and not jump. Pictures land ten times a second and the page
     draws sixty times a second, so the ghost WALKS between them: a jump every
     six frames is the stutter and means the interpolation is not running.

  5. THE ROLL-OUT MUST NOT TELEPORT THE DRIVER. When P1's bay shuts, P1's own
     truck must carry on from where it stands. If it snaps back to its spawn,
     the core was restarted in the middle of a live run and every picture after
     it is of a different run.

  6. NEITHER CHIP SAYS `not publishing`. That line is this tab's own transcript
     being refused by the node, and it comes first on the chip because nothing
     else on it can show that fault - the socket stays up and the player keeps
     driving while every watcher's picture freezes.

WHAT WOULD STILL BE A HOLE even if all six look right: the page takes the
daemons' word for the round's randomness. It refuses a round where the two of
them disagree, and it does NOT derive the beacon's height from the chain -
that is letter 32's work and the page does not do it.

## M2.36, why 19:27 and 19:31 both told the truth: the replay is flat

The 19:27 look measured each tab's picture of the other against that truck's own
core at (0.000, 0.000) m. The 19:31 look watched P2's chip crawl -100,-3 to
-97,-3 while P1 was out in the tank field. Both happened, and the difference is
the ground.

`init` leaves a core "flat until the host uploads the relief". The PAGE uploads
one - `CoreDrivenTruck.UploadGround` calls `BlwpCore.SetGround` with
`MempoolTerrain.HeightGrid`, and `UploadSolids` does the same for the boxes.
THE DAEMON'S REPLAY DOES NEITHER: `RunInProgress` calls `init(seedWord)` and
steps. Counted rather than remembered: files in `src/` that give a replay a
ground, 0.

Measured, one seed, one drive, six hundred ticks, the only difference being the
ground the core was given:

    after 20 ticks, still on the apron        0.000 m apart
    after 600 ticks   flat    (-77.322, -45.794) m
                      relief  (-65.947, -14.285) m
                                             33.500 m apart

The apron is level by construction - `MempoolTerrain.HeightAt` flattens both
ends of the map on purpose, "a metre of remaining relief anywhere under it is a
metre of daylight under one end" - so the two worlds agree EXACTLY while the
truck is standing at its bay or rolling off it. That is the whole of the 19:27
measurement: it was taken on the apron, over 3.6 m of it. The moment the truck
is on relief the replayed truck drives a different map, which is a chip that
crawls while the real truck is in the field.

IT IS NOT ONLY THE GHOST. The same replay decides the outcome and the score the
round pays on, so a run that leaves flat ground is judged in a world nobody
drove.

AND THE GROUND HAS NO HOME IN THE PROTOCOL. Checked: `contracts.js`,
`transcript.js`, `batch.js` and `checkpoint.js` carry nothing about heights,
terrain or relief. A replay cannot ask for it because there is nowhere to ask.
Worse, it is not derivable: `MempoolTerrain.HeightAt` is `Mathf.Log10` of a
LIVE mempool fee profile plus `Mathf.PerlinNoise` - a host's live data through
Unity's own float maths, which NIGHT-RUN already measured as the thing the
fixed-point core exists to avoid. No other party can reproduce it, and the page
telling the core what the world looks like is the simulator leaking back into
Unity by a door nobody was watching.

## M2.36, closed: the committee walks the same seeded hills the player drove

THE PICK WAS DANIEL'S: the core generates the relief from the round's seed, in
integer fixed-point, and Unity draws it. Trusting a client-uploaded heightfield
was rejected as an attack - a player who publishes their own hills chooses the
world they are scored in - and pinning Unity's Perlin/mempool float grid was
rejected because that is still C# simulating the ground.

WHAT WAS BUILT

  - `rng.js` gains `hash2(seedWord, i, j)`: splitmix32's finaliser over the
    three, `Math.imul` and shifts only. A FUNCTION and not a stream, because a
    stream depends on how many times it has been drawn from and the ground is
    asked about corners in whatever order a caller walks them. It lives in an
    arithmetic file because it multiplies.
  - `rules/ground.js` gains `groundFromSeed`: a 12 x 8 lattice of corner
    heights from `hash2`, bilinear across it, a second octave at half the scale
    and a quarter of the height, peak 6 m. Both ends levelled into an apron -
    level out to 86 m, easing to full relief by 66 m, with 3t^2 - 2t^3 so the
    join has no crease. `MempoolTerrain` already levelled its aprons and said
    why: an apron slab is one plane at a single height, and a metre of relief
    under it is a metre of daylight under one end. The bays are on it - 24
    doors across 156 m - and a door on a slope is a truck that rolls out of it
    sideways.
  - `sim.js`: `init` calls `groundFromSeed` where it called `flatGround`. That
    one line is the fix: the player's core and every committee's replay are the
    same function of the same seed, so they agree by construction rather than
    by agreement. `restart` no longer carries the previous ground over unless
    it was uploaded, because the seed makes a generated one again.
  - `setGround` survives for ONE caller that is not a host: the reference
    tests, which reproduce a published dataset and need the field it was
    measured on. A ground put there is marked `uploadedGround`.

WHAT WAS TAKEN AWAY, which is the half that makes it a rule

  - `BlwpSetGround` deleted from `blwp.jslib`.
  - `SetGround` deleted from `BlwpCore`.
  - `UploadGround` deleted from `CoreDrivenTruck`.
  - `HasRelief` is set by `Init` now. It used to mean "a host has uploaded
    one" and was false until it did; a core that is up always holds the round's
    hills.
  - `MempoolTerrain.HeightAt` returns `BlwpCore.SurfaceAt` when a core is
    answering. It is the one place the mesh, `SampleSurface` and the seat all
    read from, so redirecting it moves all three at once. The mempool relief
    stays below it as the answer when there is no core - the Editor, where
    PhysX drives - so the game still looks like something without a browser.

THE NUMBER

    after 20 ticks, still on the level apron    0.000 m apart   (was 0.000)
    after 600 ticks   page    (-70.212, -32.048) m
                      replay  (-70.212, -32.048) m
                                                0.000 m apart   (was 33.500)

And the world they agree on is not a table: 10176 of 15360 cells carry relief,
up to 6.930 m. Two seeds differ in 10172 of 15360 cells, so it is the ROUND's
ground and not the game's. Every bay in both rounds stands on level ground.

WHAT THE FIXTURES COST, re-measured and not adjusted. On the new ground the
daemon fixture's drive DELIVERED where it used to wreck, and those tests are
about a run that came to nothing. The world secret is the fixture's own to
choose and it chooses one where the drive still loses: `b32(0x16)` wrecks

Two core tests changed for cause. `the core drives like the PhysX truck it

### The look found a fault the suites could not, and it was a race

FIRST ROUND (db86d5c4…), at load, both pages correct: P1 seed 0x040adef9 at
bay 14 z 17.000 m, P2 seed 0x5b0fb699 at bay 22 z 71.400 m, each tab's picture
of the other equal to that truck's own core, delta (0.000, 0.000) m.

    tick  1136  P1 core ( -82.913, 10.200)  | picture ( -83.260, 17.000)  6.809 m

P1's round seed 0x040adef9 parks at bay 14, z 17.000 m - which is where the
picture put it - and P1's core was on z 10.200, which is bay 13, the harness
constant. THE PAGE WAS DRIVING THE HARNESS WORLD while the committee replayed
the round's.

The cause is an ORDER NOBODY FIXED. Two callers seed the core:
`CoreDrivenTruck.Start` calls `BlwpCore.Init(seed)` with its own constant, and
the bridge calls `core.init(seedWord)` when the join resolves. Whichever ran
last won. Both outcomes were in that one look - P2 got the bridge last and was
right, P1 got C# last and was wrong.

FIXED in `blwp.jslib`: `$blwpWorldSeed` decides it in one place, and the
argument is only a DEFAULT - once the bridge knows the round's seed, that is
the world however late anybody else asks. `BlwpInit` and `BlwpRestart` both go
through it. Pinned by a test that drives the SHIPPED jslib: after a join, two
late calls with 0x5eed1234 leave the core at the round's z -57.800 m.

The test harness had to grow with it: it bound `$blwpDiscovery` by hand, so a
new `$`-helper was a ReferenceError there and nowhere else. It binds every
`$`-prefixed member now, the way Emscripten does.

batch, 12 bytes each, MAX_INPUT_BATCH_BYTES 1835087 -> 2621509. `submitLoad` in
the core runs `rules/cargo.js`, which had ZERO CALLERS since the port while the
float copy decided the game.

AND THAT UNCALLED RULE WAS BROKEN. `Math.imul(feeSats, ONE)` wraps at 32,768
sats: a 40,000-sat bed - twice what the rule calls full - scaled to
-2,147,483,648 and clamped to ZERO, so the fattest loads would have been the
ones the war ignored. Both terms are ratios that cap at one, so the numerators
are capped first. Pinned: 20000 sats -> 65536, 40000 -> 65536, 2e9 -> 65536,
0 BTC at 2500 hundredths -> 29491, at 100000 -> 29491.

list now - `setHeat` (40), `setGround` (36), `setSolids` (39). They stay in

## 2026-09-09  M3.3 item 18 - the daemon asks the chain and pays the winner

`payWithCommittee` had zero callers in `src/`. Measured at the start, by
reading the source rather than remembering it: one file could ask the chain
about outputs (`pool-watch.js`), and nothing called the payer, so a close wrote
PAYOUT_QUEUED and stopped. Every winner in every test was paid by the test
handing the daemon an outpoint.

`Payouts.settleQueued` is the caller. `PoolSigning.owes` is split out of
`spendFor` so the asker can size an output before it has one, rounded UP -
`payoutOutputs` floors each row and drops sub-floor ones, so the transaction
pays at most the bound, and a bound a satoshi short costs a whole signing round
to discover.

WHO ASKS: `askerFor(roundId, seats)`, seats in store order (by pubkey, which no
seat chooses), indexed by four bytes of the round id. 200 rounds asked all 7
seats. A round id of 0xfffffffe would have picked seats[-x] without the `>>> 0`.

ON AN ISOLATED REGTEST (`tools/settle-regtest.mjs`), seven daemons on seven
sockets, one share each, and no outpoint given to anybody:

    the round names seat 7 of 7, and 7 of 7 seats agree
    unfunded pool         refused: 0 confirmed outputs cover the 1000 sats
    funded, in a mempool  refused: the same sentence, and it is the right one
    1 conf against 6      refused: 1 output with fewer than 6 confirmations
    6 of 6 other seats    waited; 0 transactions sent
    the asker             sendrawtransaction -> a txid, block 202 carries it

## 2026-09-09  M3.3 item 19 - a payout outlives its asker, and one spend lands

MEASURED BEFORE ANY OF IT WAS WRITTEN, because the answer decided the design.
Two askers over one output, `PoolSigning.live` still a Map:

    asker A and asker B, same process     signature SAME, raw bytes SAME
    asker B after a RESTART               signature DIFFERENT, raw DIFFERENT

Same txid both times, because a segwit txid does not cover the witness - so
this is witness malleability rather than a lost satoshi, and the money would
have gone to the same outputs either way. It is still two valid transactions
for one input, which is what a takeover must not create. The nonce pair is a
`pool_nonces` row now; the same probe after the change reads SAME / SAME.

THE CLOCK. The round's beacon height, which is not a new time source: a round
with no randomness beacon cannot be seeded, so every seat already holds the
same number. TAKEOVER_BLOCKS = 2. Seat k in `askerOrder` may ask at
beacon + k*2. The order is the seats the store keeps sorted BY PUBKEY, rotated
by four bytes of the round id - a hash of a contract signed before the round
ran, so a node cannot grind its way up. 7 seats, one eligible at the beacon and
one more every 2 blocks; handing the list round the other way gives the same
ring.

Rejected and why: wall clock (per-node; two seats a minute apart both take
over) and the pool output's own confirmations (a pool funded before the round
closes is already deep, so every seat is eligible at once).

TWO FAULTS CAME OUT OF THE WIRING, neither foreseen:

  THE COMMITMENT LIST WAS WHOEVER ANSWERED FIRST. `payWithCommittee` broke out
  of its loop at the first five, so two askers assembled two different lists -
  and the list goes into the binding factors and therefore into the challenge,
  so every seat that had already signed refused the second by name ("has signed
  under another commitment list"). All seats are asked now and the five are the
  lowest ids: one list whoever asks, at the cost of two more requests. The
  chosen ids printed 1,2,3,4,5 for every asker afterwards.

  A SEAT THAT HAD PAID REFUSED TO COMMIT AT ALL. `spendFor` demands
  PAYOUT_QUEUED, and the seat that broadcasts marks its own row PAID - so the
  takeover could not reassemble the same five, and a spend dropped from a
  mempool would have stranded the round. A seat holding a pair for that round
  answers about it whatever its row says; the sighash is still checked against
  the pair, so it relaxes nothing about starting a spend.

  And a third, one layer up: after the five became the lowest ids, the asker's
  own seat was asked for a share even when it was not in the list it had built,
  and "this seat is not in the commitment list" was reported as a withdrawal.

ON AN ISOLATED REGTEST (`tools/settle-regtest.mjs`), the asker never run:

    the order survives being handed round the other way: true
    height 201   6 of 6 seats waited, nothing broadcast, row still queued
                 "may ask at height 202; the chain is at 201, 1 block past"
    height 202   the next seat took over, 5 of 5 signed
                 sendrawtransaction -> a txid, block 203 carries it
                 the winner's own key holds 1000 sats
    same instant the seat behind, that spend still in the MEMPOOL:
                 "that output is already going: the chain holds no such
                 unspent output" - `gettxout` sees a mempool, `scantxoutset`
                 does not, which is why the takeover re-reads through it
    its own turn the seat behind: refused, the pool holds nothing
    after a restart  the asker came back and spent nothing
    on the chain the winner's key holds 1000 sats - ONE payment, not two

TWO HARNESS CHECKS WERE TRUE SENTENCES ABOUT THE WRONG THING and were fixed
rather than kept: the seat behind was being stopped by the CLOCK, not by the
output being spent, so it now waits for its own turn first; and the mempool
window is only open before a block is mined, so that probe moved to the instant

alone from the parity of a key computed from public data, and it is the move

because a test that only saw even keys would pass with the normalisation

declined it" and "the wallet was never asked" look the same from the outside;
the fake wallet records every request so the difference is a figure.

NIP-04 AND NOT NIP-44, named in the file. NIP-47 was specified over NIP-04 and
it is what wallets in the field still accept; NIP-44 is newer and some now
prefer it. AES-256-CBC over the ECDH x-coordinate through WebCrypto - the same
door `seal.js` opens for AES-GCM, and the same agreement `page-curve.ecdhShared`
already computes for the sealed VSS shares. No new dependency. `page-curve`
gained `signSchnorr`: the one operation NIP-01 needs, and the page had no reason
to sign on this curve before - its session key is Ed25519 and the player key was
only ever a public point.

SUBSCRIBE BEFORE PUBLISH. The wallet answers as soon as it sees the request, so
a client that published first and listened afterwards would miss an answer that
arrived in between - on a fast relay, most of them. The event id is known before
it is sent, so the filter can name it.

TWO COLLISIONS THIS REPO ALREADY KNEW ABOUT caught the first draft: `subtle` is
declared at the top level of `seal.js` too, and `tools/bundle.js` refuses two
private names that collide (the same guard the `fromHex` duplicate tripped); and
`discovery.test.js` refuses any `globalThis.` in blwp-client/src - a client that
reads anything off the page is a client that can be told where to send things -
so the crypto and the socket are reached the way `fetch` and `WebSocket` already
are in the neighbouring file.

NOT PLAYER-FACING. Nothing in index.html pastes a connection, shows the amount,
or shows the running total §24A.1 requires. That is the next line, deliberately:
a screen that quotes money it cannot take is worse than no screen. PlayMode and
EditMode are not in this letter - no C# changed.
